# OpenAI-Compatible Bridge

> **Cost note**: by default the bridge drives the Claude Code CLI, so usage counts against your Claude account. It does not bypass Anthropic's billing or subscription limits. Heavy agent traffic can consume extra-usage credits at API rates. Check your usage at [claude.ai/settings/usage](https://claude.ai/settings/usage).

The embedded server (`clawo serve`, or the OpenClaw plugin) exposes a drop-in OpenAI-compatible endpoint so any client that speaks `/v1/chat/completions` can talk to a persistent Claude Code (or Codex / Antigravity / Grok Build) session; the request's `model` picks the engine — see [Model routing](#model-routing). The bridge is designed to serve **two kinds of clients as first-class citizens**:

1. **Upstream agents** that maintain their own conversation state and forward only the latest user turn — OpenClaw's main agent loop, cron jobs, subagents, programmatic clients.
2. **OpenAI-compatible webchat / labeling tools** that re-send the full transcript on every turn — ChatGPT-Next-Web, Open WebUI, LobeChat, data-labeling pipelines.

Both modes share the same wire protocol; the difference is how a "new conversation" is detected. See [Operator Modes](#operator-modes) below.

## Endpoint

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     |
| ----------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **URL**                 | `http://127.0.0.1:18796/v1/chat/completions` (`clawo serve --port` / `--host`, or `OPENCLAW_SERVER_HOST`, change the address)                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       |
| **Models endpoint**     | `GET /v1/models` — the model registry, as an OpenAI model list                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      |
| **Inspection endpoint** | `GET /v1/sessions` (lists active openai-compat sessions with caching stats)                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         |
| **Auth**                | `Authorization: Bearer <token>`. By default the server reuses the token in `~/.openclaw/server-token`, or generates one and writes it there (mode 0600). Set `OPENCLAW_SERVER_TOKEN=<value>` to choose the token, or `OPENCLAW_SERVER_TOKEN=disabled` to turn auth off. The token grants full control, so see [Security model](./getting-started.md#security-model) |
| **Wire format**         | OpenAI Chat Completions, both streaming (SSE) and non-streaming                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     |
| **Usage**               | `usage` (on the final chunk when streaming) counts this request's tokens — what the turn added to the session's running totals, which `GET /v1/sessions` reports                                                                                                                                                                                                    |
| **Default model**       | `claude-sonnet-4-6` when the request has no `model`                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 |

The request fields the bridge reads are `model`, `messages`, `stream`, `user` and `tools`. `max_tokens` is
validated (it must be a positive number) but does not limit the reply; `temperature` and other sampling fields are
ignored — the CLI runs with its own settings.

A streamed reply opens with a `role` chunk, sends a `: keepalive` comment every 30 seconds while the turn runs,
ends with a chunk carrying `finish_reason` (and `usage`, when available), then `data: [DONE]`. When
the request carries `tools`, the reply is held back until the turn finishes, so the tool calls can be parsed out of
it, and then sent as `tool_calls` chunks (finish reason `tool_calls`) or as one content chunk — on every engine,
whether or not it streams deltas.

## Model routing

The `model` field picks the engine as well as the model, through the registry in `src/models.ts`:

1. **`agy/<model>`** runs `<model>` on Antigravity (`agy`).
2. **A registered id or alias** runs on the engine it is registered to — `opus`, `sonnet`, `haiku` and the
   `claude-*` ids on `claude`, the `gpt-*` ids, `o3`, `o4-mini` and `codex-mini-latest` on `codex`, Antigravity's
   Gemini ids on `agy`, `grok` and the `grok-*` ids on `grok`. `GET /v1/models` lists the current ones.
3. **An unregistered name** falls back on its prefix: `gpt*`, `o3*`, `o4*` and `codex*` run on `codex`, `grok*` on
   `grok`.
4. **Anything else** — including vendor-prefixed names such as `anthropic/claude-sonnet-4-6` — runs on `claude`,
   with the name passed through.

Two legacy engines are still reachable this way: the registry's `gemini-*-preview` ids (aliases `gemini-pro`
and `gemini-flash`) and any unregistered name containing `gemini` run on `gemini`, and `composer-*`, `cursor*`
and `auto` run on `cursor`. Nothing else selects an engine, so `opencode`, `codex-app`, `acp` and custom
engines are not reachable through the bridge.

## Session keying

Each request is mapped to a long-running session. Once a session exists, subsequent requests with the same key reuse the same persistent CLI subprocess — so Anthropic prompt caching warms across turns. The key is derived in priority order:

1. **`X-Session-Id` header** — explicit, highest precedence
2. **`user` field in the request body** — OpenAI standard field, treated as a stable caller identifier
3. **`sys-<sha1(model + systemPrompt + tools)[0..12]>`** — automatic fallback so unkeyed callers don't all collapse onto a single shared session
4. **`'default'`** — only when there is no system prompt, no model and no tools (degenerate empty body)

Without the hash fallback, unkeyed callers (for example OpenClaw's main agent, cron jobs and subagents behind one gateway) would share one session: their requests would queue behind each other and could receive another caller's system prompt.

The model is mixed into the hash so that two callers with the same system prompt but different requested models (e.g. one wants `opus`, another wants `sonnet`) get separate sessions rather than responses from the wrong model.

The full plugin-side session name is `openai-<key>`. The key becomes a directory
name — the bridge starts each session in `~/.claw-orchestrator/compat/<name>`, a
directory of mode 0700 that must belong to the server's user —
so a key that is not 1–64 characters of `[A-Za-z0-9._-]` without `..` is replaced
by a hash of itself (`k-<16 hex>`). An ordinary id is used unchanged; a key
containing path separators cannot choose where the session runs.

The tool list is fingerprinted into the hash fallback by name, the first 64
characters of the description, and the **parameter schema** (with object keys
normalised, so a re-serialised identical schema still resolves to the same
session). On the Claude engine the schemas are written into the session's system
prompt when the session is created and are not re-sent per turn, so a changed
schema has to resolve to a new session for the model to see it. An explicit key
(`X-Session-Id` or `user`) carries no fingerprint — see
[Known limitations](#known-limitations).

### How a bridge session runs

- **Working directory**: the empty temp directory above, so the CLI picks up no
  project files, `CLAUDE.md` or git state from wherever the server was started.
- **Permission mode**: `bypassPermissions`.
- **On `claude`**: with `tools` in the request, the CLI's own built-in tools are
  switched off (`--tools ""`) and its system prompt is replaced
  (`--system-prompt`) by a preamble that says it has no tools of its own, the
  tool definitions (sent in each message instead under
  `OPENAI_COMPAT_TOOLS_PER_MESSAGE`), and the caller's system prompt. Without `tools`, the caller's
  system prompt is appended (`--append-system-prompt`). Either is fixed when the
  session is created.
- **On the other engines**: the caller's system prompt and the tool definitions
  travel in the message; see [Tool definitions](#tool-definitions-and-where-they-live).
- **Compaction**: before a turn on an existing session whose context is over 80%
  full, the bridge compacts it.
- **Persistence**: bridge sessions are not written to the on-disk session
  registry. An idle session is stopped when its TTL runs out and is not resumed.

## Operator modes

### Default mode — agent / programmatic clients

When `OPENAI_COMPAT_NEW_CONVO_HEURISTIC` is **not `1`**, the bridge assumes upstream callers maintain their own conversation transcript and only forward the latest user turn. A session is reused for as long as it lives — until it sits idle past its TTL. The only signal that starts a new conversation is the explicit reset header:

```
X-Session-Reset: 1
```

(also accepted: `true`, case-insensitive, with whitespace)

When the header is present, the existing session for this key is stopped and a fresh one is created. Use this from a client that wants "new chat" semantics under your own control — e.g. when your UI's "Clear History" button is pressed.

A turn treated as a new conversation (the reset header, or the webchat heuristic below) runs in a session that is stopped as soon as it has answered. The next request for the key starts another session and replays whatever earlier turns its `messages[]` carries (see [Conversation history](#conversation-history-on-the-way-in)). A client that forwards only its latest turn carries none, so the reset turn's exchange is not in that session.

### Webchat mode — `OPENAI_COMPAT_NEW_CONVO_HEURISTIC=1`

When the env var is set to `1`, the bridge additionally restores a legacy heuristic: a request whose `messages` array contains exactly one non-system message (i.e. the conversation has no assistant turns yet) is treated as a fresh conversation. This is the only signal that webchat frontends (ChatGPT-Next-Web, Open WebUI, LobeChat) emit when the user clicks "New Chat" — they clear their UI transcript and post `[system, user]`.

Without this flag, those frontends would silently continue the previous CLI session and surface stale context the user thought they had cleared.

Set it in the server's environment. It is read per request, but a running process does not see a later `launchctl setenv` or shell export, so restart the server after changing it.

| Mode              | Best for                                                    | New-conversation signals                            |
| ----------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------- |
| **Default**       | OpenClaw main agent, cron jobs, subagents, scripted clients | `X-Session-Reset: 1` only                           |
| **`HEURISTIC=1`** | ChatGPT-Next-Web, Open WebUI, LobeChat, data labeling tools | `X-Session-Reset: 1` **and** `[system, user]` shape |

## Status webhook

When `OPENAI_COMPAT_STATUS_URL` is set to a plain `http://` URL, each chat completion sends best-effort `POST` requests with `Content-Type: application/json` and body:

| Field      | Type           | Meaning                                                                                                                     |
| ---------- | -------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `state`    | string         | `thinking` (turn started), `working` (a tool is running), or `idle` (turn finished or failed).                              |
| `activity` | string         | Short human-readable line, e.g. `Processing request...`, `Reading: foo.ts`, `Running: npm test`, `Ready`, `Request failed`. |
| `tool`     | string \| null | Tool name when `state === working`, otherwise `null`.                                                                       |

Failures are ignored (no retries) and never affect the completion: a request the endpoint has not answered within 2 s is dropped, and a URL the bridge cannot POST to — anything but `http://`, or malformed — sends nothing. Use this from a small local HTTP handler that forwards status into your webchat UI.

## Tool definitions and where they live

When the request carries `tools`, the schemas have to reach the CLI somehow. Which
mechanism is used depends on whether the engine keeps the conversation itself.

| Engine                                       | Turn 1                                                        | Later turns                                                                                                                                           |
| -------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `claude`                                     | Schemas go into the session system prompt (`--system-prompt`) | Nothing injected — the system prompt persists                                                                                                         |
| `codex`, `agy`, `grok` (and legacy `cursor`) | Full schema block prepended to the message                    | A short reminder of the calling convention, no schemas — but only once the conversation id has been captured; until then the full block is sent again |
| legacy `gemini`                              | Full schema block prepended to the message                    | Full schema block again — it has no resume surface, so nothing persists between sends                                                                 |

The engines in the middle row resume a conversation by id, so everything injected
stays in the transcript. Re-sending the full block each turn would grow the prompt
without bound (a 54-tool block is roughly 17k tokens), so a few turns could
overflow the context window. The short reminder is still needed, because the
block carries the "emit a tool call, do not carry out the work yourself" framing;
without it the CLI starts doing the work directly.

A fresh session always gets the full block, so a thread is never created without
the definitions — including when a session was evicted and is being recreated. A
caller with no explicit key (no `X-Session-Id`, no `user`) that changes its tool
list mid-conversation also gets the full block, because the tool list is part of
the hashed key, so a different list resolves to a different session. With an
explicit key it does not — see [Known limitations](#known-limitations).

## Inspection: `GET /v1/sessions`

Returns a JSON list of every active OpenAI-compat session and its caching statistics:

```bash
TOKEN=$(cat ~/.openclaw/server-token)
curl -s http://127.0.0.1:18796/v1/sessions -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" | jq
```

Sample response:

```json
{
  "object": "list",
  "data": [
    {
      "key": "sys-a3f81c9d0b27",
      "session_name": "openai-sys-a3f81c9d0b27",
      "model": "claude-opus-5-5",
      "cwd": "/home/me/.claw-orchestrator/compat/openai-sys-a3f81c9d0b27",
      "created": "2026-04-09T03:12:18.441Z",
      "turns": 68,
      "turns_succeeded": 14,
      "tokens_in": 248312,
      "tokens_out": 38201,
      "cached_tokens": 198104,
      "context_percent": 28,
      "cost_usd": 0.4123
    }
  ]
}
```

`turns_succeeded` is one per request; `turns` is not comparable to it on these
sessions — the Claude CLI emits a `user` event per tool-result batch and `turns`
counts those, so the gap above is tool use, not failures. Compare
`turns_succeeded` against your own request count.

The single most important field is **`cached_tokens`**. If it grows turn-over-turn, the persistent CLI is being reused and Anthropic prompt caching is warming. If it stays at 0, something is killing the session every turn — check that no client is sending `X-Session-Reset` unintentionally and that `OPENAI_COMPAT_NEW_CONVO_HEURISTIC` is not set when it shouldn't be.

```bash
curl -s http://127.0.0.1:18796/v1/sessions -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" | jq '.data[] | {key, model}'
# Expected: two new rows with distinct keys, one claude-opus-5-5 and one claude-sonnet-5-5.
```

**3. `X-Session-Reset: 1` resets cleanly.**

```bash
SID=smoke-reset
curl -s http://127.0.0.1:18796/v1/chat/completions \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -H "X-Session-Id: $SID" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"model":"opus","messages":[{"role":"user","content":"remember the word banana"}]}' > /dev/null
curl -s http://127.0.0.1:18796/v1/chat/completions \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -H "X-Session-Id: $SID" -H "X-Session-Reset: 1" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"model":"opus","messages":[{"role":"user","content":"what word did I just tell you"}]}' \
  | jq -r '.choices[0].message.content'
# Expected: model says it has no prior context.
```

**4. `cached_tokens` grows turn-over-turn (the success metric).**

```bash
SID=smoke-cache
PREAMBLE=$(printf 'x%.0s' {1..3000})
for i in 1 2 3 4; do
  curl -s http://127.0.0.1:18796/v1/chat/completions \
    -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -H "X-Session-Id: $SID" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
    -d "{\"model\":\"opus\",\"messages\":[{\"role\":\"system\",\"content\":\"long preamble: $PREAMBLE\"},{\"role\":\"user\",\"content\":\"turn $i\"}]}" > /dev/null
  curl -s http://127.0.0.1:18796/v1/sessions -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
    | jq ".data[] | select(.session_name == \"openai-$SID\") | {turn: $i, cached_tokens, tokens_in}"
done
# Expected: cached_tokens climbs substantially by turn 3-4. If it stays at 0,
# the persistent CLI is still being killed every turn — regression.
```

## Error responses

Errors from the bridge itself use the OpenAI error envelope:

```json
{ "error": { "message": "...", "type": "invalid_request_error" } }
```

| Status | `type`                  | When                                                                                          |
| ------ | ----------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| 400    | `invalid_request_error` | `messages` empty/missing, no user message, invalid `max_tokens`                               |
| 404    | `invalid_request_error` | Unknown `/v1/*` path                                                                          |
| 503    | `server_error`          | Failed to start a new session (session limit reached, model unavailable, CLI crashed at boot) |
| 502    | `upstream_error`        | The CLI finished the turn with an error                                                       |
| 500    | `server_error`          | Mid-turn failure                                                                              |

The checks that run before a request reaches the bridge answer in the server's own shape,
`{ "ok": false, "error": "..." }`:

| Status | When                                              |
| ------ | ------------------------------------------------- |
| 400    | Body is not valid JSON                            |
| 401    | Missing or wrong bearer token (when auth enabled) |
| 413    | Request body over 5 MiB                           |
| 415    | POST without `Content-Type: application/json`     |
| 429    | Rate limited (`OPENCLAW_RATE_LIMIT` exceeded)     |

A streamed request has already received `200` by the time the turn runs, so a turn that ends in an error
(`upstream_error`) or fails mid-turn (`server_error`) arrives as a `data: {"error": {...}}` frame followed by
`data: [DONE]`.

# Sessions

Sessions are the core abstraction — persistent, multi-turn coding conversations backed by a coding CLI. `claude`, `codex-app`, `acp` and a persistent `custom` engine keep one process alive for the whole session; the one-shot engines (`codex`, `agy`, `grok`, `opencode`) start a process per send and resume their conversation by its id.

## Lifecycle

```
startSession() → sendMessage() → sendMessage() → ... → stopSession()
```

A session that sits idle past the memory TTL is unloaded, and one whose server restarts is gone from memory. Both stay in the resume registry for 7 days, and `startSession()` with the same name resumes the conversation. `stopSession()` ends a session for good: it removes the registry entry too, so the same name later starts a new conversation. See [Session Persistence](#session-persistence).

### Starting a Session

```typescript
const info = await manager.startSession({
  name: 'my-task',
  cwd: '/path/to/project',
  model: 'opus', // alias or full name
  permissionMode: 'acceptEdits',
  effort: 'high',
  allowedTools: ['Bash', 'Read', 'Edit', 'Write'],
  maxTurns: 50,
  maxBudgetUsd: 5.0,
});
```

Starting a name that is already live returns that session's info unchanged. The number of live sessions is capped by `maxConcurrentSessions` (default 5; 32 under `clawo serve`).

Key options:

| Option               | Description                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         |
| -------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `engine`             | `'claude'` (default), `'codex'`, `'codex-app'`, `'agy'`, `'grok'`, `'opencode'`, `'acp'` (with `acpAgent`), or `'custom'` (with `customEngine`) — see [Multi-Engine](./multi-engine.md)                                                                                                                                                                                             |
| `model`              | Model alias (`fable`, `opus`, `sonnet`, `haiku`, `agy-pro`, `agy-flash`, `grok`) or full name. A non-Claude model on the `claude` engine goes through the [multi-model proxy](#multi-model-proxy)                                                                                                                                                                                   |
| `permissionMode`     | `acceptEdits` (default), `bypassPermissions`, `plan`, `auto`, `manual`, `dontAsk` (`default` = legacy alias for `manual`)                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           |
| `effort`             | `low`, `medium`, `high`, `xhigh`, `max`, `ultra`, `auto` (default) — each engine clamps to its own ladder (see [Multi-Engine](./multi-engine.md))                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   |
| `sandboxMode`        | `read-only`, `workspace-write`, `danger-full-access`. `codex` and `codex-app` support all three (default `workspace-write`); `read-only` is enforced on `claude`, `agy`, `grok` and `opencode` through their own read-only modes; a custom engine must map it or the session refuses to start; an `acp` session refuses `read-only`, because the agent's tools run inside the agent |
| `maxBudgetUsd`       | Spend cap in USD, checked before every send on every engine; once spend reaches it, further sends are refused                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       |
| `bare`               | Claude Code: skip hooks, LSP, auto-memory, CLAUDE.md                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                |
| `worktree`           | Claude Code: run in an isolated git worktree                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        |
| `appendSystemPrompt` | Append custom instructions to the system prompt. Claude Code and Grok take it natively; Codex, Antigravity and OpenCode have no such flag and receive it at the top of the first message of a conversation, as does `codex-app` on a new thread and an `acp` session on a new session                                                                                               |

### Sending Messages

```typescript
const result = await manager.sendMessage('my-task', 'Fix the auth bug', {
  effort: 'high', // override effort for this message
  plan: true, // ask for a plan only (claude and persistent custom engines)
  timeout: 600_000, // 10 min timeout (default 5 min)
  onChunk: (text) => process.stdout.write(text), // streaming
});

console.log(result.output);
```

Sends to one session run one at a time: a second `sendMessage()` waits for the first to finish. `plan` puts a plan-only instruction in front of the message and leaves the permission mode unchanged; start the session with `sandboxMode: 'read-only'` to enforce it. The result carries `output`, the engine's resume id as `sessionId`, `error` when the engine reported the turn as failed, and `permissionDenials` / `images` when the turn had any.

`SendOptions` also accepts `parentRunId`, `nodeKind` and `taskKind`, all stamped onto the turn's run ledger row ([observability.md](./observability.md)). `taskKind` is caller-declared and never inferred from the prompt.

### Session Persistence

A session is recorded in the resume registry, `~/.openclaw/claude-sessions.json` (the directory can be moved with `CLAWO_SESSIONS_DIR`), once its engine has reported a resume id:

- **Memory TTL**: an idle session is unloaded after `sessionTtlMinutes` (default 120; 60 under `clawo serve`). Its registry entry stays.
- **Disk TTL**: 7 days since the last activity.
- **Auto-resume**: `startSession` with a registered name resumes that conversation, restoring its engine, model, working directory, `sandboxMode`, `autoCompactPercent` and `chrome`. Other options — permission mode, tool lists, system prompts — are not stored; pass them again.
- **Not recorded**: sessions started with `noSessionPersistence`, and sessions whose engine has not reported a resume id yet.

### Session Resume & Fork

```typescript
// Resume a conversation by the engine's own id
await manager.startSession({
  name: 'continued',
  resumeSessionId: 'abc123-session-id',
});

// Claude Code and Grok: fork it for experiments (preserves history, new branch)
await manager.startSession({
  name: 'experiment',
  resumeSessionId: 'abc123',
  forkSession: true,
});
```

`resumeSessionId` is the id the engine itself uses: a Claude Code session id, a Codex or `codex-app` thread id, an Antigravity conversation id, a Grok or OpenCode session id, an ACP agent's session id, or a custom engine's id when its config maps a resume flag. `forkSession` becomes `--fork-session` on Claude Code and Grok; it is a `SessionManager` option and not a `session_start` tool parameter.

> `claude continue/respawn/stop/logs` are not headless subcommands — session continuation is via `resumeSessionId`/`forkSession`. Use the `claude_agents_list` tool (`claude agents --json`) to enumerate Claude Code background agent sessions.

### Handing off to another engine

`resumeSessionId` and `forkSession` continue a conversation on the engine that holds it. To continue
it somewhere else — a stuck Claude session into Codex, an expensive model into a cheaper one —
use `handoffSession` (tool: `session_handoff`):

```typescript
await manager.handoffSession('refactor', {
  engine: 'codex',
  message: 'Carry on from where we stopped.', // optional: send now and return the reply
});
// → new session 'refactor-codex', same cwd; 'refactor' keeps running untouched
```

`newName` names the new session (default `<name>-<engine>`) and `model` picks its model (default:
that engine's default). The result reports the new session's `name` and `engine`, what was carried
as `carried: { turns, omitted, chars }`, and the reply as `result` when `message` was given. A
session with no recorded exchange yet cannot be handed off.

**How the conversation travels.** No engine can resume another's session, and each keeps its
history in its own undocumented on-disk format. So the conversation is replayed as text: a
`<conversation_history>` block in front of the new session's first message, after which the new
engine holds it itself. Every turn in it is fenced, so a reply that contains the block's own tags
cannot close it early and speak as another role. Nothing is written into either engine's session
store.

**What carries across.** What was said: every message sent through `sendMessage` and every reply,
recorded per session as it happens. The session's own history buffer is not used for this — it is
capped by event count, and on a long session the opening request is the first thing it loses. The
new session inherits the source's working directory and its engine-neutral settings (permission and
sandbox mode, effort, spend cap, auto-compact threshold, system prompts, extra directories). It does
not inherit anything written for the source engine — its model, tool allowlists in that engine's
tool names, resume ids, profiles.

**What does not.** The source engine's hidden reasoning, which no engine exposes, and the detail of
tool calls — the new agent sees the replies that described the work, and the workspace itself, which
the framing tells it to check before relying on anything the history describes.

**When it is too long.** Up to `maxChars` (default 240,000 characters, ~60k tokens; minimum 4,000)
the whole conversation is sent. Past that, the opening request is kept, the newest turns fill what
is left, and one line records how many turns in between were left out: the request says what the
work is for, the newest turns say where it stands, and the middle is what the workspace can answer.

**A fork, not a move.** The two sessions go their separate ways. The new one starts from the
source's record, so handing it off again carries the whole conversation rather than only its own
part. The history is cleared only after a first send succeeds, so a first turn that fails on the
new engine does not strand the conversation it was carrying.

### ultracode (Claude dynamic workflows)

Set `ultracode: true` on a Claude `session_start` to have Claude orchestrate a JS workflow per substantive task and fan out to subagents. It is injected as the `ultracode: true` settings key merged into `--settings`:

```typescript
await manager.startSession({ name: 'big-task', engine: 'claude', ultracode: true });
```

A workflow runs in the background, so `session_send` returns once it is launched — the reply is
Claude saying so, not the workflow's result. When the workflow finishes, Claude Code starts a turn of
its own to report it. That turn answers no send: it is never returned as the reply to a later
`session_send`, it does not count toward `turnsSucceeded`, and its cost is included in the session's
spend. The same holds for any turn the session did not send, such as a message from another Claude
Code session. Read the outcome by sending a follow-up once the workflow has had time to finish.

### Codex app-server turn control (`engine: 'codex-app'`)

Mid-turn and thread control via the Codex app-server v2 RPCs, surfaced as tools: `codex_interrupt` (cancel the in-flight turn), `codex_steer` (add input without restarting), `codex_fork` (branch the thread), `codex_rollback` (drop the last N turns), `codex_models` (list models + supported reasoning efforts), `codex_thread_list` (list the threads the session can see).

The same engine carries Codex's `/goal`: set and manage it on a session with the `codex_goal_*` tools, or run it as a checked workflow — goal, then verify, then repair on the same thread — with the `goal` node and `clawo goal` ([workflow.md](./workflow.md#goal)).

### Fan-out (cross-engine parallel)

`fanout_start` runs one task across N engine/model agents in parallel and collects their answers (optional synthesis) — the best-of-N / diverse-perspective primitive. Unlike Council, no rounds/votes/worktrees; use Council for isolated parallel edits. See [tools.md](./tools.md#fanout_start).

Each agent is a session and counts against `maxConcurrentSessions`. Fan-out and Council run no more agents at once than there are free slots when they start, and the rest wait for an agent to finish. When no slot is free at all, the agents fail on the cap rather than wait for sessions they do not own. On a memory-constrained host, the cap is the knob that bounds how many engine processes run at once. An aborted fan-out starts none of the agents still waiting.

## Runtime Operations

### Model Switching

Switch models mid-conversation with `switchModel()` (tool: `session_switch_model`). The session restarts on the new model and resumes the engine's own conversation by its resume id, so history is preserved:

```typescript
await manager.switchModel('my-task', 'haiku'); // fast model for simple tasks
await manager.switchModel('my-task', 'opus'); // back to powerful model
```

The switch is refused while a turn is running, for a model the registry does not know (a `provider/model` string is accepted), and for a session with no resume id yet — except `agy`, which then restarts fresh. If the restart fails, the session is restarted with its old configuration and the call throws. `setModel()` only changes the stored model, which takes effect at the next restart.

### Claude Account Rotation

A `claude` session on an account in the server's rotation (`claudeAccount`) moves to another account
on its own: when the account refuses a turn at its usage limit, or before a turn once the account is
near it. The CLI process restarts under the new account's credential and resumes the same
conversation by its session id, so history is kept, and a refused turn is sent again. The session's
status names the account it runs under. See [multi-engine.md](./multi-engine.md#claude-accounts-and-rotation).

### Tool Management

Add/remove tool permissions at runtime with `updateTools()` (tool: `session_update_tools`), which restarts the session the same way:

```typescript
await manager.updateTools('my-task', {
  allowedTools: ['Bash', 'Read'],
  merge: true, // add to the existing lists
});

await manager.updateTools('my-task', {
  removeTools: ['Bash'], // drop Bash from both lists
  merge: true, // keep the rest of each list
});
```

Without `merge: true` both lists are replaced, so a list you omit is cleared — including on a call that only passes `removeTools`. The busy and resume-id guards of `switchModel()` apply here too.

### Context Management

```typescript
// Compact to reclaim context window
await manager.compactSession('my-task', 'We fixed the auth bug, now working on tests');

// Check context usage
const status = manager.getStatus('my-task');
console.log(`Context: ${status.stats.contextPercent}%`);
```

`contextPercent` is how full the live context is right now — the current turn's
prompt over the window the engine actually enforces — so it rises and falls with
the conversation. A persistent `custom` engine is the exception: there it is the
session's cumulative tokens over the engine config's `contextWindow` (200,000 when
unset), so it only grows (and a one-shot `custom` engine reports 0).
`stats.tokensIn` is the different question of how many input tokens the session
has been billed for in total, which only ever grows.

`compactSession()` runs `/compact` (with the optional summary) on `claude` and a
persistent `custom` engine, and starts the thread's own compaction on `codex-app`.
It is a no-op on the one-shot engines whose CLI has no compaction command (`codex`,
`agy`, `grok`, `opencode`), which log a warning the first time it is called, and a
silent no-op on `acp` agents, which manage their own context, and on one-shot
`custom` engines.

A long-lived session can compact itself: start it with `autoCompactPercent`
(1–99, off by default) and, before each send, the session is compacted first
if `contextPercent` has reached that value. Every call in a turn re-reads the
whole context from cache, so cost grows with context size; compacting earlier
trades detail of older turns for cheaper ones. The setting survives a restart
of the server, and a failed compaction never costs the send.

```typescript
await manager.startSession({ name: 'assistant', cwd: '/srv/bot', autoCompactPercent: 85 });
```

`stats.turns` and `stats.turnsSucceeded` are the same kind of distinction.
`turns` counts turns that reached the engine, whatever their outcome, including
the ones that then failed. `turnsSucceeded` counts only the ones the engine
reported as successful, and it is one per send on every engine.

**The two are only comparable on the one-shot engines.** There `turns` is also
one per send, so the difference between them is the failure count. On `claude`
and a persistent `custom`, `turns` counts `user` events — and the CLI emits one
per tool-result batch as well as the prompt echo, so a send that used eight tools
counts nine. Compare `turnsSucceeded` against the number of sends there, never
against `turns`.

Which outcome counts as a success is the engine's own verdict, not the exit
code's: `codex` fails a turn that emits `turn.failed` while exiting 0, `agy`
requires a `SUCCESS` status, a zero exit _and_ a non-empty reply (it can report
success and then die in cleanup), `codex-app` requires `status: 'completed'` so a
turn cancelled through `interrupt()` does not count, an `acp` agent must end the
turn with the stop reason `end_turn`, `opencode` refuses a turn on purpose when
read-only enforcement did not load, and the legacy `gemini` engine succeeds on
exit 53 because its turn limit resolves.

**A succeeded turn is not a turn that did the work.** When the engine refuses a
tool call it usually does not fail the turn. On Claude Code with
`--permission-prompts none` — which a session gets whenever no prompt tool is
configured — a turn asked to write a file came back `subtype: 'success'`,
`is_error: false`, with the refused Bash call listed in the result event and no
file on disk. It counts in `turnsSucceeded` and sets no `error`. The refused calls
reach the caller as `permissionDenials` on the send result; read that before
treating a successful turn as work done.

The run ledger's `ok` reads this same counter, so a turn cannot be a failure on
`/v1/sessions` and a success in `clawo runs`.

## Multi-Model Proxy

Built-in format translation lets Claude Code CLI talk to non-Anthropic models:

- **Anthropic ↔ OpenAI** bidirectional message/tool conversion
- **Streaming SSE** format conversion
- **Gemini** schema cleaning (removes unsupported JSON Schema keys)
- **Gemini** thought signature caching (round-trip thinking)
- Auto-detect provider from model name patterns

A `claude` session started with a non-Claude model and no `baseUrl` starts the proxy on a local port and points the session at it, unless `CLAWO_CLAUDE_GATEWAY=1` says the caller's own gateway serves that model (see [Multi-Engine](./multi-engine.md)). Configuration is in the proxy section of [Multi-Engine](./multi-engine.md); see [`src/proxy/`](https://github.com/Enderfga/claw-orchestrator/tree/main/src/proxy) for implementation details.

## Circuit Breaker

SessionManager tracks consecutive failures per engine type. After 3 consecutive start failures for an engine, a circuit breaker opens with exponential backoff (1s × 2^(n-1) after the n-th consecutive failure, capped at 5 minutes). During backoff, new session creation for that engine is rejected with a descriptive error.

- Resets on successful session start
- State visible in the `health()` response (the `sessions_overview` tool) under `circuitBreakers`
- Constants: `CIRCUIT_BREAKER_THRESHOLD` (3), `CIRCUIT_BREAKER_BACKOFF_BASE_MS` (1s), `CIRCUIT_BREAKER_MAX_BACKOFF_MS` (5 min)

## Orphaned Process Cleanup

If the process that owns the sessions exits without stopping them, their engine processes can outlive it. When a session starts, SessionManager records the PID of its engine process in `~/.openclaw/session-pids.json`, together with its own PID, and cleans up on startup:

1. Reads the PID file left by earlier runs
2. Skips entries whose owning SessionManager is still alive, and old-format entries that name no owner
3. For each remaining PID, checks if the process is alive (`kill -0`)
4. Verifies the process command line names a known engine binary — `claude`, `codex`, `agy`, `grok`, `opencode`, or the legacy `gemini` / `cursor-agent` / `agent` — so a recycled PID is never killed
5. Sends SIGTERM to the process group and the process, then SIGKILL after 3 seconds
6. Rewrites the PID file without the stale entries

The one-shot engines have no process running when a session starts, so they have no PID to record. ACP agents and persistent custom engines are recorded, but their binaries are not in the known list, so an orphaned one is left running.

## Stats & Monitoring

Session stats are `manager.getStatus(name).stats`, surfaced through `coding_session_status`.

Claude Code–specific stats:

| Field                 | Type                                   | Description                                                                                                                               |
| --------------------- | -------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `retries`             | number                                 | Total API retries that occurred during the session (present on every engine; only Claude Code reports retries)                            |
| `lastRetryError`      | string \| undefined                    | Error category of the most recent retry (e.g. `overloaded`, `rate_limit`), or its HTTP status when the CLI gives no category              |
| `pluginErrors`        | `Array<{plugin, reason}>` \| undefined | Plugins that failed to load due to unmet dependencies, captured from the `system/init` event. `undefined` when no plugin errors occurred. |
| `refusalFallbacks`    | number \| undefined                    | Turns the model refused and the CLI re-ran on another model (`system/model_refusal_fallback`). `undefined` when none happened             |
| `lastRefusalFallback` | `{from, to, category?}` \| undefined   | The most recent of those: the refusing model, the model that re-ran the turn, and the refusal category when the CLI reports one           |

### `system/api_retry` events

When Claude Code CLI performs an API retry (transient errors, overload, etc.) it emits a `system` event with subtype `api_retry`. The plugin parses these events and increments `retries` / updates `lastRetryError` in the session stats. These events are also visible in the session event history returned by `session_grep`, which holds the session's last 100 events.

```typescript
const status = manager.getStatus('my-task');
console.log(`Retries so far: ${status.stats.retries}`);
if (status.stats.lastRetryError) {
  console.log(`Last retry reason: ${status.stats.lastRetryError}`);
}
```

## ISession.pid

All session engine classes expose an optional `pid` readonly property, providing the OS process ID of the underlying CLI subprocess. Returns `undefined` when no process is running — on the one-shot engines, between sends. SessionManager reads it for [orphan cleanup](#orphaned-process-cleanup) and does not expose it; read it from an engine class you construct yourself:

```typescript
import { PersistentClaudeSession } from '@enderfga/claw-orchestrator';

const session = new PersistentClaudeSession({ name: 'probe', cwd: '/path/to/project', permissionMode: 'acceptEdits' });
await session.start();
console.log(session.pid); // e.g., 12345
```

## Verifying what a session did

A plain session leaves no verdict — it ran, and nothing checked the result. To
check it, hand `verify_run` a contract and the directory:

```jsonc
verify_run({
  cwd: "/repo",
  contract: { checks: [{ type: "command", cmd: "npm", args: ["test"] }] }
})
```

For work that should be checked as part of running it, use a workflow instead —
see [`workflow.md`](./workflow.md).

survives a process restart and can be resumed.

Codex `/goal` on one `codex-app` thread, then the contract, then repairs on the same thread; see
[workflow.md](./workflow.md#goal).

### `workflow_status`

`{ runId, events? }` → run state, per-node status, `outcome`, `outcomeReason`,
`verdict`, `evidenceId`, `costUsd`, `consensusVotes`, and the last N events when
`events` is given.

`outcome` is `verified` (a contract passed), `refuted` (it failed), or
`unverified` (**nothing checked the work**, which is not the same as a failure):
either no contract was declared, or a pass no longer stands because the tree
changed after it or an abandoned attempt was still running, in which case
`outcomeReason` says why. `verdict` is the most recent verifier result: its node,
`evidenceId` and the tree digest it was taken at.

### `workflow_list` / `workflow_resume` / `workflow_cancel` / `workflow_steer` / `workflow_approve`

- `workflow_list({ workflow?, state?, limit? })` — newest first (`limit` default 25), survives
  restarts. `state` is one of `pending`, `running`, `awaiting_human`, `verifying`, `completed`,
  `failed`, `cancelled`.
- `workflow_resume({ runId, agentCustomEngineRefs? })` — nodes already succeeded are not re-run;
  the node that was in flight is retried, because a half-finished node left no result to trust.
  A run whose agents used a custom engine needs `agentCustomEngineRefs`
  (`{ "<agent>": "<REF>" }`, resolved from `CLAWO_CUSTOM_ENGINE_<REF>` on the orchestrator's host).
- `workflow_cancel({ runId })` → `{ cancelled }`.
- `workflow_steer({ runId, text })` → `{ steered }` — the text is **prepended** to the next agent
  node's prompt. Steers not yet consumed are delivered after a restart too.
- `workflow_approve({ runId, approved })` — answers a `human_gate` node. A run
  parked before the server restarted is resumed with the answer attached, so it
  needs no separate `workflow_resume`. Returns `{ answered: false }` when the run
  is not parked at a gate.

### `verify_run`

Run an acceptance contract against a directory outside any workflow — for a plain
`session_send` that edited a repo, say. `{ cwd, contract, baseSha?, label? }` →
the evidence bundle, stored under `~/.claw-orchestrator/wf/<label>/evidence/`. A
`label` that is the id of an existing workflow run is refused.

Without `baseSha`, `diff_policy` sees untracked files only. `verify_run` has no record of
the tree before the work, so `protectTests` does not apply to it. It runs the checks once and
spawns no repair session, so `fixOnFailureRounds` does not apply either.

### The `contract` parameter

```jsonc
{
  "id": "ship-it",
  "fixOnFailureRounds": 2,
  "checks": [
    { "type": "command", "cmd": "npm", "args": ["test"], "timeoutMs": 600000 },
    { "type": "command", "cmd": "npm", "args": ["run", "lint"], "required": false },
    { "type": "http", "url": "http://localhost:3000/health" },
    { "type": "screenshot", "url": "http://localhost:3000/", "viewports": [{ "width": 1440, "height": 900 }] },
    { "type": "diff_policy", "forbidPaths": ["configs"], "maxFiles": 40 },
    { "type": "file", "path": "dist/index.js" },
  ],
}
```

`protectTests` (default on) refutes a workflow run whose test files or test configuration
changed during it; set it to `false` when changing tests is the task. See
[verification.md](./verification.md#protected-tests).

**Declare it yourself.** Never copy a contract out of an agent's output: an agent
that writes its own acceptance criteria is grading itself, which is the problem
contracts exist to solve. Unrecognised fields are dropped before anything runs,
and a `command` check is argv — there is no shell string to inject into.

`required` defaults to true; a failing non-required check is recorded in the
evidence bundle without refuting the run.

`screenshot` captures and stores images. It does not compare pixels and is not
visual regression testing.

# Ultraplan & Ultrareview

High-level orchestration features for deep project planning and fleet code review. Inspired by Claude Code's Ultraplan and Ultrareview commands.

## Ultraplan

A dedicated planning session that explores your project thoroughly (up to 30 minutes) and produces a detailed implementation plan.

### How It Works

1. Starts an Opus session in **plan mode** with **max effort**
2. Appends a system prompt instructing thorough exploration and plan-only output
3. Sends the task description and waits for completion
4. Returns the plan text when done

Runs in background — poll with `ultraplan_status`.

### Usage

```typescript
const plan = await manager.ultraplanStart('Add OAuth2 support with Google and GitHub providers', {
  cwd: '/path/to/project',
  model: 'opus', // default
  timeout: 1800000, // 30 min default
});

console.log(`Plan ID: ${plan.id}`);

// Poll for completion
const status = manager.ultraplanStatus(plan.id);
if (status?.status === 'completed') {
  console.log(status.plan);
}
```

### Tools

| Tool               | Description                         |
| ------------------ | ----------------------------------- |
| `ultraplan_start`  | Start planning session (background) |
| `ultraplan_status` | Get status and plan text            |

### Configuration

| Parameter | Default               | Description                  |
| --------- | --------------------- | ---------------------------- |
| `model`   | `opus`                | Model to use for planning    |
| `cwd`     | `process.cwd()`       | Project directory to explore |
| `timeout` | 1,800,000 ms (30 min) | Maximum planning time        |

Results are stored as a durable run and remain queryable after a restart.

## Ultrareview

A set of specialized reviewer agents that review your codebase in parallel, each from a different angle. Built on the fan-out primitive (see `fanout_start` in [tools.md](./tools.md)).

### How It Works

1. Starts a fan-out of N reviewer agents (1-20, default 5)
2. Each agent reviews from a different angle in the project directory, read-only on every engine (`sandboxMode: 'read-only'`, and plan mode on Claude), so no reviewer can change the code it is reviewing
3. Agents run in parallel; one failing reviewer does not stop the others
4. A read-only synthesis pass merges all findings into one report

### Available Review Angles (20)

| Agent               | Focus                                                    |
| ------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------- |
| SecurityReviewer    | Injection, auth flaws, data exposure, OWASP top 10       |
| LogicReviewer       | Off-by-one, race conditions, null handling, edge cases   |
| PerformanceReviewer | O(n^2) loops, memory leaks, missing caching, N+1 queries |
| APIReviewer         | Inconsistent interfaces, missing validation, error gaps  |
| TestReviewer        | Untested paths, missing edge case tests, flaky patterns  |
| TypeReviewer        | `any` casts, unsafe assertions, missing null checks      |
| ConcurrencyReviewer | Race conditions, deadlocks, async error handling         |
| ErrorReviewer       | Swallowed errors, missing try/catch, crash paths         |
| DependencyReviewer  | Outdated packages, CVEs, unnecessary deps                |
| ReadabilityReviewer | Unclear naming, complex functions, dead code             |
| DataReviewer        | Data validation, schema mismatches, encoding             |
| ConfigReviewer      | Hardcoded values, missing env vars, insecure defaults    |
| ScalabilityReviewer | Single points of failure, unbounded growth               |
| DocReviewer         | Outdated docs, missing API docs, misleading comments     |
| A11yReviewer        | ARIA labels, keyboard nav, color contrast                |
| I18nReviewer        | Hardcoded strings, locale handling, RTL support          |
| NetworkReviewer     | Missing timeouts, retry logic, connection pooling        |
| AuthReviewer        | Token handling, CSRF, permission checks                  |
| CryptoReviewer      | Weak algorithms, key management, RNG                     |
| MemoryReviewer      | Memory leaks, circular references, stream handling       |

### Usage

```typescript
const review = await manager.ultrareviewStart('/path/to/project', {
  agentCount: 10, // use 10 of the 20 angles
  maxDurationMinutes: 15, // 15 min timeout per agent
  model: 'sonnet', // model for all reviewers
  focus: 'Find security and performance bugs',
});

console.log(`Review ID: ${review.id}`);

// Poll for completion
const status = manager.ultrareviewStatus(review.id);
if (status?.status === 'completed') {
  console.log(status.findings);
}
```

| Tool                 | Description                        |
| -------------------- | ---------------------------------- |
| `ultrareview_start`  | Launch reviewer fleet (background) |
| `ultrareview_status` | Get status and findings            |

# Verification — acceptance contracts and evidence

An **acceptance contract** is a list of checks the runtime executes itself and
whose results it reads. A run that declares one is judged by its last
verification: it ends `failed` when a required check of that verification fails,
and `completed` / `verified` only when every required check passes.
Completion signals that come from an agent or an engine (consensus votes, a
Coder's reported metric, an engine's `ok`) are recorded, but they are never
treated as verification.

## The one rule about where contracts come from

**A contract comes from the caller or from a mode default. Never from agent
output.** If an agent could declare its own checks, we would be back to
self-grading with more steps. Nothing in the kernel reads a contract out of a
node's result.

The `contract` argument of `workflow_start`, `POST /workflow/new` and `verify_run`
goes through `normalizeContract()`, which drops anything it does not recognise, so
it carries no fields the executor did n

side a git repository the digest is unavailable. Nothing running after the
  checks means the verdict stands; something running after it means we decline
  to vouch, and the run says so.
- If an abandoned attempt (a node past its timeout, which cannot be killed) is
  still running when the run ends, the outcome is `unverified` with the reason
  recorded. The runtime will not vouch for a tree something may still be writing
  to.

What it is **not**: a promise that nothing can touch the tree after a run ends.
A node past its timeout keeps running, and if it outlives the short settle
window its writes land after the last digest — the run will have said
`unverified`, but the file is still changed. Give such nodes a timeout they will
not hit, or make their writes safe to arrive late.

# Workflow kernel — durable runs

A durable executor for workflow runs: what is running, what happens when a step
fails, when to stop, and how to come back after the process dies.

## Every mode runs on it

`workflow_start` runs a spec you write or a [built-in template](#built-in-templates);
`clawo solve`, `clawo fanout` and `clawo goal` start the same templates from a
terminal. The mode tools run on the same kernel: `council_start`, `fanout_start`,
`ultraplan_start`, `ultrareview_start` and `autoloop_start` each create a kernel
run, and so does an UltraApp build. The modes' result shapes — `CouncilSession`,
`FanoutSession`, `UltraplanResult`, `UltrareviewResult`, `AutoloopState` — are
_projected_ from the run record, so `workflow_list` lists every one of them.

The mode engines (`Council`, `Fanout`, the autoloop planner/coder/reviewer
dispatcher) do the work; the kernel owns lifecycle, persistence and listing. A
run's record stays on disk until you delete it.

## Durability contract

Every state transition i

  waits briefly for outstanding attempts to settle, and reports `unverified`

- Cancel and a node timeout are different things. A timeout is a node failure

- Nothing prunes run directories. Delete a run that is not executing yourself
